newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, MD say antitrust concerns not "big issue".
newsitem.headline: Boeing, MD say antitrust concerns not "big issue".

text.p: Anti-trust concerns will not be "a big issue" in the $13.3 billion merger of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp, Boeing chief executive Phil Condit said at a news conference here Sunday.
"We looked very carefully at all of our programs," Condit said. "We believe that dramatically they are complementary. There are some overlaps but they're very, very minor."
"In the military and space areas, we're absolutely complementary," McDonnell Douglas chief executive Harry Stonecipher said. "There's plenty of competition in this arena."

The newly merged company will be headquartered in Seattle, Washington, but the company also planned to continue operations at existing major locations, including St Louis, Missouri, the executives said.

"We're going to keep the major operating locations right where they are," Condit said. "In a growing environment, there may be some reassignments to handle that growth but that will allow us to minimize the need for layoffs."
The companies plan to complete the merger by mid-1997, Condit said.

"Our best guess, and I underline the word guess because there are a lot of other agencies that have to be involved, (is) that the process will be at least a six-month kind of process," Condit said. "So mid-year is sort of the target area. It could be a little shorter."
The merger took shape quickly after a meeting between the two top company executives last Tuesday, Condit said. "The deal was really cut in the last week," he said.
The companies have not had an opportunity yet to discuss the anti-trust issues with U.S. government regulators, Condit said. "Clearly, we've not spoken to people at this point," he said.
The companies will continue producing competing commercial aircraft, including the Douglas Aircraft line, Stonecipher said.
"We intend to continue the lines of products that we currently have going at Douglas," Stonecipher said.
"We will continue to sell those product lines. It will really be the marketplace that will decide on which of those airplanes get sold," he said.
Previously announced plans to have McDonnell Douglas personnel work on Boeing aircraft in Long Beach, California, will go forward, Stonecipher added.
John McDonnell, chairman of McDonnell Douglas, said he would retire from his post effective February 1, 1997 as he had previously announced.

"But I will remain on the board for an interim period to try to help with this transition," McDonnell said at Sunday's news conference. "After that period, it would not be my intention to remain on the board for an indefinite period."

Frank Shrontz, chairman of Boeing, said he would also retire. "One of my major responsibilities that I took on as chairman was to look at overall industry restructuring and restructuring of our company," Shrontz said.
"I would say this has satisfied that major objective of mine and I'm ready to retire."
